Model-Based Kappa for Ordinal Ratings from Many Raters

Source: R/ord_kappa_test.R
ord_kappa_test.Rd

Estimates the model-based kappa \(\kappa_m\) of Nelson and Edwards (2015) and Nelson, Mitani and Edwards (2017), and please cite these papers if this function is utilized. This is a chance-corrected measure of exact agreement between raters who classify subjects on an ordinal scale. It is computed from an ordinal (cumulative probit) generalized linear mixed model with crossed random effects for subjects and raters, so it describes the populations of raters and subjects that were sampled, and it is not affected by the prevalence of the categories.

Requires the ordinal package.

Usage

ord_kappa_test(
  x = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  measure = NULL,
  item = NULL,
  id = NULL,
  col.names = NULL,
  categories = NULL,
  conf.level = 0.95,
  null.value = NULL,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "greater", "less"),
  group = NULL,
  group_type = c("rater", "subject")
)

Arguments

x

A formula of the form rating ~ rater | id. Leave NULL to use measure, item and id (long data) or col.names (wide data).

data

A data frame.

measure, item, id

Names of the columns with the ratings, the raters, and the subjects (long data).

col.names

Names of the columns with each rater's ratings (wide data, one row per subject).

categories

All categories of the ordinal scale, in order. Defaults to the levels of a factor, and otherwise to the sorted observed ratings. Character ratings need categories to set their order. The number of categories, C, enters \(\kappa_m\) through the chance agreement 1/C.

conf.level

Confidence level of the interval (default 0.95).

null.value

The hypothesized value of \(\kappa_m\), in [0, 1). NULL (default) gives no test. Not used with group.

alternative

The alternative hypothesis: "two.sided" (default), "greater" or "less". Without a null.value the interval is two-sided.

group

Optional name of a column with a two-level rater or subject characteristic (e.g. experienced or inexperienced raters, younger or older patients), constant within each rater (or subject). The two groups are then compared; see Details. The order of the levels is that of a factor, and otherwise sorted. Requires long data.

group_type

Whether group describes the "rater"s (default) or the "subject"s.

Value

A list of class c("cac_htest", "htest") containing:

statistic

The z statistic (only with a null.value), or with group, the likelihood ratio statistic.

p.value

The p-value (only with a null.value or group).

conf.int

The confidence interval for \(\kappa_m\), or with group, for the difference between the groups (second minus first).

estimate

The estimated \(\kappa_m\), or with group, one per group.

stderr

The delta-method standard error(s).

null.value

The hypothesized value.

alternative

The alternative hypothesis.

method

A description of the method.

data.name

A description of the data.

fit

The fitted model (model), the variance components (sigma2_subject, sigma2_rater), rho and its standard error, the thresholds, the observed agreement at the fitted thresholds (p0), the number of categories C, the rater conditional modes and their conditional variances (rater_effects), and the numbers of subjects and raters. With group, fit also has the null model (null_model), the likelihood ratio test (lrt), the fixed effect of the group (beta), one variance per group, and a table of subgroup kappas with standard errors and intervals (subgroups).

data

The ratings in long format.

settings

The settings used, for the methods.

Details

Model. The rating of subject i by rater j falls in category c when a latent variable falls between thresholds \(\alpha_{c-1}\) and \(\alpha_c\): $$P(Y_{ij} \le c \mid u_i, v_j) = \Phi(\alpha_c - u_i - v_j),$$ with subject effects \(u_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_u)\) and rater effects \(v_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2_v)\). It is fitted by the Laplace approximation with ordinal::clmm().

Kappa. Observed agreement \(p_0\) is the probability that two raters put the same subject in the same category. Chance agreement is taken at its minimum, \(p_c = 1/C\), reached when the thresholds split the latent scale into C equally likely categories, and \(p_0\) is evaluated at those thresholds. Then $$\kappa_m = \frac{p_0 - 1/C}{1 - 1/C},$$ which depends only on C and \(\rho = \sigma^2_u / (\sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_v + 1)\), the share of the latent variance due to differences between subjects. \(\kappa_m\) is 0 when \(\rho = 0\) and approaches 1 as \(\rho\) approaches 1. Because the thresholds drop out, \(\kappa_m\) does not depend on how common each category is. The observed agreement at the fitted thresholds is also returned (fit$p0).

Inference. The standard error is from the delta method with the covariance matrix of the variance components from the model Hessian (Nelson et al., 2017). The interval and test are formed on the logit of \(\rho\) and mapped back to \(\kappa_m\), so the interval stays within [0, 1]; Nelson et al. (2017) used the Wald interval \(\hat\kappa_m \pm 1.96\, se\), which can be found from estimate and stderr. The p-value is from a z test of \(\rho = \rho_0\), where \(\rho_0\) gives the null.value of \(\kappa_m\).

Design. Raters and subjects are treated as random samples from their populations. Missing ratings are allowed. At least three raters are needed to estimate the rater variance (Nelson et al., 2017); with few raters or subjects the variance components, and so the interval, are imprecise.

Comparing groups. With group, the group enters the model as a fixed effect (shifting the thresholds, e.g. for a higher prevalence of severe ratings in older patients), and the rater (or subject) variance may differ between the two groups (Nelson et al., 2017). The result gives \(\kappa_m\) within each group, with an interval for their difference, and the test is the likelihood ratio test of a common variance. For rater groups, fit$subgroups also gives \(\kappa_m\) between a rater from each group; chance agreement is then minimised numerically over common thresholds, and the fixed effect matters. Subgroup intervals are formed on the logit scale.

Nelson et al. (2017) add a random slope for the group indicator and test its variance and correlation against a 50:50 mixture of chi-square distributions with 1 and 2 df. Because the group is constant within each rater (or subject), only the variance in each group is identified, not the intercept-slope covariance, and the Hessian of that model is singular. The equivalent model with a separate variance for each group is fitted instead: it has the same likelihood and the same kappas, with one parameter fewer. Equal variances lie inside its parameter space, so the likelihood ratio statistic is compared with a chi-square distribution with 1 df.

References

Nelson, K. P., & Edwards, D. (2015). Measures of agreement between many raters for ordinal classifications. Statistics in Medicine, 34(23), 3116-3132. doi:10.1002/sim.6546

Nelson, K. P., Mitani, A. A., & Edwards, D. (2017). Assessing the influence of rater and subject characteristics on measures of agreement for ordinal ratings. Statistics in Medicine, 36(20), 3181-3199. doi:10.1002/sim.7323

See also

cac_htest-methods for summary() and plot(); cac_test() for Gwet's AC1/AC2, Fleiss' kappa and Krippendorff's alpha.

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("ordinal", quietly = TRUE)) {
  # Simulated ratings of 60 subjects by 8 raters on a 5-point scale
  set.seed(42)
  d <- expand.grid(id = 1:60, rater = paste0("R", 1:8))
  latent <- rnorm(60, sd = 1.5)[d$id] + rnorm(8, sd = 0.5)[d$rater] +
    rnorm(nrow(d))
  d$rating <- cut(latent, c(-Inf, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, Inf), labels = FALSE)
  res <- ord_kappa_test(rating ~ rater | id, data = d)
  res
  summary(res)
  plot(res, type = "raters")

  # Do the first 4 raters agree better than the other 4?
  d$exp <- ifelse(d$rater %in% c("R1", "R2", "R3", "R4"), "exp", "inexp")
  res_g <- ord_kappa_test(rating ~ rater | id, data = d, group = "exp")
  res_g
  res_g$fit$subgroups
}
#>       subgroup   kappa_m         se     lower     upper
#> 1          exp 0.2784536 0.03412541 0.2166932 0.3499522
#> 2        inexp 0.2545958 0.03882608 0.1861483 0.3377664
#> 3 exp vs inexp 0.2658583 0.03431574 0.2041858 0.3382412
# }
